title: 1996 Air Africa crash
summary: Moscow Airways Antonov An-32B overran the runway while attempting to take off fully fueled and overloaded from N'Dolo Airport's short runway. The aircraft failed to achieve sufficient speed to bring its nose up, began to lift, and crashed into the Simbazikita produce market. The full fuel load ignited, creating a massive post-impact fire. Ground fatalities were estimated between 225 and 348, making this the deadliest aviation accident in African history and deadliest by ground casualties outside of terrorist attacks.
probable_cause: The aircraft was overloaded and fully fueled while attempting to take off from N'Dolo Airport's short runway. The aircraft did not achieve sufficient speed to bring its nose up yet began to lift prematurely, resulting in loss of control and crash into the market below.

Aircraft overran the runway at N'Dolo Airport.

title: LAC Colombia 028
summary: A Douglas DC-8 stalled and crashed minutes after takeoff from Luque, Paraguay. The pilot improperly ceded control to a novice co-pilot shortly after departure and then turned off two engines as a test, without proper authority or qualifications. The co-pilot struggled with the aircraft configuration, and both left engines were shut down at 500 feet. Carburator explosions indicated the aircraft could not climb on reduced power, and when pilots attempted to reactivate engines, they did not react in time to prevent impact with a soccer field in Mariano Roque Alonso.
probable_cause: Pilot error: improper transfer of control to unqualified co-pilot, unauthorized shutdown of two engines under uncontrolled conditions, lack of safety doctrine in the cockpit, and failure to recognize and recover from the resulting aircraft stall.

factors.evidence: pilot improperly gave control of the plane to his co-pilot, a novice, and began to test the engines
Probable execution of unauthorized take-off training under uncontrolled conditions and by a person not qualified as an instructor
pilot gave control of the plane to the co-pilot, a novice, a prohibited procedure that made the aircraft operation difficult
Little experience of the pilot in command in this function
Two carburetion explosions were heard, indicating that the aircraft was forced to climb so that no air could enter the other engines
The plane fell to the ground, crashing into a playing field around 2 km from the end of the runway

events.text: The aircraft took off around 2:30 p.m. from Luque Airport, bound for Campinas.
A few minutes after takeoff, the pilot gave control of the plane to his co-pilot, a novice, and began to test the engines.
One of the left engines was first turned off, causing the aircraft to bank.
Another engine was then turned off at 500 feet while the co-pilot retook control of the plane and attempted to climb with two engines turned off.
Two carburetion explosions were heard, indicating that the aircraft was forced to climb so that no air could enter the other engines, meaning that the engines could not operate at full power.
The plane fell to the ground, crashing into a playing field around 2 km from the end of the runway in the Mariano Roque Alonso district, killing the four Colombian crew members and 18 other people.

title: Birgenair 301

agencies.name: Dominican Republic General Directorate of Civil Aviation

summary: Birgenair Flight 301, a Boeing 757 chartered from Puerto Plata to Frankfurt, crashed into the Atlantic shortly after takeoff on 6 February 1996, killing all 189 aboard. Investigators concluded a pitot tube, likely blocked by a wasp nest after the aircraft sat idle for 20 days without its covers, fed the captain's airspeed indicator false and increasing readings while the first officer's showed the correct, decreasing speed. Confused by conflicting overspeed and stall warnings, the captain reduced thrust believing the plane was too fast, triggering the stick shaker and a stall from which the crew did not recover.
probable_cause: The probable cause was the flight crew's failure to recognize and react to a blocked captain's pitot tube, most likely obstructed by a wasp nest, which produced erroneous, increasing airspeed indications that led the crew to reduce thrust into an aerodynamic stall.

factors.evidence: One of the three pitot tubes used to measure airspeed was blocked, most likely by a mud dauber wasp nest built inside it.
The aircraft had sat unused for 20 days, and its pitot covers were removed two days before the accident for an engine test run.
The captain's airspeed indicator showed over 300 knots and increasing while the first officer's correctly showed 220 knots decreasing.
Confused by the contradictory readings, the captain reduced thrust believing the aircraft was flying too fast.
The reduced thrust immediately triggered the 757's stick shaker stall alert.
The pilots should have followed existing procedures and aborted the takeoff once their airspeed indicators showed significant disagreement.
As the plane neared a stall its path became unstable and it started descending.

events.text: During the takeoff roll at 23:42 the captain found his airspeed indicator malfunctioning but chose not to abort the takeoff.
The autopilot engaged one minute 30 seconds into the flight; about ten seconds later rudder ratio and Mach airspeed trim warnings appeared.
The captain's ASI showed over 300 knots and increasing while the first officer's showed 220 knots decreasing, and an overspeed warning sounded.
Climbing through 4,700 ft with his ASI reading 350 knots, the confused captain reduced thrust, believing the plane too fast.
The reduced thrust immediately triggered the stick shaker stall alert, and the autopilot disengaged as the aircraft neared a stall.
As the plane became unstable and began descending, the controller called the flight and the first officer only replied "Stand by."

title: Faucett 251
summary: Faucett Perú Flight 251 crashed on approach to Arequipa at night after the crew received an outdated barometric altimeter setting. The aircraft impacted terrain 2 kilometers short of the runway, with the crew unaware they were flying nearly 1000 feet lower than displayed.
probable_cause: Crew issued outdated barometric altimeter setting after bypassing ILS signal, causing altitude misjudgment and controlled flight into terrain during night approach in poor visibility.

factors.evidence: the crew had been issued an outdated barometric altimeter setting after bypassing an ILS signal

The airplane crashed into hills at 8200 ft, approximately 2 km short of the runway

events.text: The aircraft was on a VOR/DME approach to Rodríguez Ballón International Airport's runway 09, at night, in rain and mist, with thunderstorms reported in the area.
The flight crew asked for the lights of the runway to be brightened as they could not see them when they should on normal approach.

It was found that the crew had been issued an outdated barometric altimeter setting after bypassing an ILS signal, causing them to fly almost 1000 ft lower than the altitude they believed they were flying at.
The airplane crashed into hills at 8200 ft, approximately 2 km short of the runway.

summary: A Learjet 25D collided with Serra da Cantareira near São Paulo during approach. The crew was fatigued from an extended work period and exhibited poor coordination. ATC communication was compromised by improper phraseology, and the crew was unfamiliar with destination airport procedures. Darkness and low visibility prevented terrain detection.

Environmental factors of darkness and reduced visibility enabled the impact.

title: 1996 Croatia USAF CT-43 crash
summary: United States Air Force Flight IFO-21, a Boeing CT-43A executive transport, was carrying Secretary of Commerce Ron Brown and 34 others. While attempting an instrument approach to Dubrovnik Airport on an NDB non-precision approach, the aircraft strayed off course and crashed into a mountainside. The investigation determined failure of command, aircrew error, and an improperly designed instrument approach procedure. The aircraft lacked one of two required ADFs and the approach was not approved for Department of Defense aircraft.
probable_cause: The investigation board determined failure of command, aircrew error and an improperly designed instrument approach procedure. The particular NDB approach used required two operating ADFs, but this aircraft only had one ADF installed. The approach was not approved for Department of Defense aircraft.

factors.evidence: many American pilots are not fully proficient in performing NDB approaches; a NASA survey showed that 60% of American transport-rated pilots had not flown an NDB approach in the last year

While NDB approaches are essentially obsolete in the United States, they are still used widely in other parts of the world, and the aircraft crashed into terrain during approach

events.text: The aircraft was on an instrument flight rules non-directional beacon NDB approach to Runway 12 when it strayed off course.
The aircraft passed the final approach fix at 80 kn above the proper approach speed.
The crash site on a 2,300 ft hill was 1.6 mi northeast of where the aircraft should have been on the inbound course to the NDB.

title: ValuJet 592
summary: ValuJet Flight 592 crashed into the Florida Everglades about ten minutes after departing Miami on May 11, 1996. A fire developed in the cargo compartment caused by 144 expired chemical oxygen generators placed in cargo compartment boxes marked COMAT by maintenance contractor SabreTech. The fire caused progressive failure of the DC-9's electrical and flight control systems. All 110 people on board were killed, making it the deadliest aviation accident in Florida history.
probable_cause: Just before takeoff, 144 expired chemical oxygen generators were placed in the cargo compartment by ValuJet's maintenance contractor SabreTech, which violated Federal Aviation Administration regulations. The fire in the cargo compartment caused progressive failure of electrical and flight control systems leading to loss of control and crash.

title: Garuda Indonesia 865
summary: Garuda Indonesia Flight 865 aborted takeoff from runway 16 at Fukuoka Airport after the number 3 engine failed at speeds nearing V2. The abort occurred after nose rotation, and despite use of brakes, ground spoilers and thrust reversers, the aircraft could not stop within runway boundaries. The aircraft overran the runway 620 meters, striking a ditch, fence and road, resulting in structural damage that caused post-impact fire.
probable_cause: Engine failure during takeoff at critical speed, with abort decision at rotation speed. The final report determined pilot error and failure of the airline's maintenance and flight operation sections to properly coordinate maintenance intervals resulted in the accident. The engine turbine blades had been in service for 6,182 cycles when General Electric recommended discarding after 6,000 cycles.

title: 1996 Belgian Air Force Hercules accident
summary: Belgian Lockheed C-130 Hercules encountered a flock of starlings during approach to Eindhoven Airport on 15 July 1996. The birds were ingested into the two left engines, causing the aircraft to lose power and overshoot the runway. Post-crash fire destroyed the cockpit and forward fuselage, killing 34 of 41 people aboard. Investigation found that passenger information was not transmitted to destination airport, delaying emergency response.
probable_cause: Ingestion of common starlings into the two left engines caused the aircraft to go out of control during landing.

title: TWA 800
summary: TWA Flight 800, a Boeing 747 flying from New York to Rome via Paris, exploded in flight and crashed into the Atlantic Ocean off East Moriches, New York, twelve minutes after takeoff on 17 July 1996, killing all 230 aboard. The four-year NTSB investigation concluded that flammable vapors in the center fuel tank ignited, likely from a short circuit, after finding arcing in the fuel quantity indication system wiring that enters the tank; the captain had remarked on 'crazy' FQIS readings shortly before the explosion.
probable_cause: The NTSB determined the probable cause was an explosion of flammable fuel/air vapors in the center wing fuel tank, most likely ignited by a short circuit, with evidence of arcing found in the fuel quantity indication system wiring that enters the tank.

factors.evidence: Problems with the aircraft's wiring were found, including evidence of arcing in the fuel quantity indication system (FQIS) wiring that enters the tank.
The report's conclusion was that the probable cause of the accident was the explosion of flammable fuel vapors in the center fuel tank.
Several wide-ranging recommendations were made, which were incorporated into newer US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) standards.
The Boeing 747-100 performing this flight exploded and crashed into the Atlantic Ocean near East Moriches, New York, twelve minutes after takeoff.

events.text: About two minutes and thirty seconds before the explosion, the captain remarked about 'crazy' readings from the fuel quantity indication system.
At approximately 8:31 p.m. EDT, twelve minutes after takeoff, the Boeing 747 exploded and crashed into the Atlantic Ocean near East Moriches, New York.
NTSB investigators found evidence of arcing in the fuel quantity indication system wiring that enters the center fuel tank, a likely ignition source for the flammable vapors.
All 230 people on board were killed when the aircraft broke apart and crashed into the ocean, the deadliest air disaster investigation in U.S. history up to that time.
The four-year NTSB investigation approved its Aircraft Accident Report on August 23, 2000, and its recommendations were incorporated into new FAA fuel-tank safety standards.

title: Vnukovo Airlines 2801
summary: On approach to Svalbard Airport, the crew used outdated Jeppesen charts and set both HSIs to magnetic runway heading 283 degrees without using the localizer course. During the inbound turn, lateral deviation from the centerline grew due to inadequate wind drift correction. The aircraft reached Advent at 1,524 meters and turned late, resulting in a left (northeast) deviation from the correct track. Navigation at 1,524 m minimum altitude led to aircraft striking ground at Operafjellet during final approach, 3.7 km from the centerline.
probable_cause: A series of small navigational errors caused the aircraft to be 3.7 km from the approach centerline at the time of impact. The crew did not attempt to intercept the correct magnetic course and were probably not aware of VHF direction finding available at the airport.

title: Aeroperú 603
summary: Aeroperú Flight 603 experienced total loss of airspeed, altitude, and vertical speed indications due to adhesive tape left covering the static ports after maintenance. Flying at night over water without visual references, the crew received contradictory warnings and struggled to control the aircraft. Multiple stalls occurred during descent from an unknown altitude, and the aircraft eventually crashed into the Pacific Ocean.
probable_cause: Maintenance worker left adhesive tape covering the static ports after aircraft cleaning. This blocked the ports critical to all basic flight instruments, providing false and contradictory data to the flight crew and flight computers, preventing accurate control during the approach.

title: TAM Transportes Aéreos Regionais 402
summary: TAM Flight 402 encountered an uncommanded thrust reverser deployment on the right engine while climbing away from runway 17R at Congonhas. The safety cable preventing reverser actuation parted at a maintenance connection when the copilot held the throttle fully open. With the right engine producing reverse thrust and the left engine at takeoff power, the aircraft rolled violently to the right and descended into buildings and houses only 25 seconds after takeoff.
probable_cause: The safety system cable parted at a maintenance connection because it could not withstand simultaneous tension from the reverser actuator pulling in one direction while the copilot held the throttle lever in the opposite direction, allowing uncommanded thrust reverser deployment during climb and causing asymmetric thrust and loss of control.

title: ADC Airlines 86
summary: ADC Airlines Flight 086 was descending to 16000 ft when Triax Flight 185 was assigned a conflicting altitude at 15000 ft. The Lagos ATC controller made a radar separation error, thinking Flight 086 was at 10000 ft when it was actually descending to 16000 ft. Flight 086's TCAS warned of traffic and the crew attempted evasive action. Following the TCAS alert, Captain Sama took control, but ATC directed a heading that led to loss of control and the aircraft crashed inverted in Lagos Lagoon at high speed.
probable_cause: Air traffic control separation error combined with loss of control during evasive maneuver.

title: Charkhi Dadri mid-air collision
summary: Saudia Flight 763, a Boeing 747 climbing out of Delhi, collided almost head-on over Charkhi Dadri on 12 November 1996 with Kazakhstan Airlines Flight 1907, an Ilyushin Il-76 descending toward Delhi, killing all 349 aboard both aircraft. The Lahoti Commission found the Kazakh crew, relying on a radio operator due to poor English skills, failed to level off at their assigned altitude and kept descending toward the Saudia jet, compounded by crew resource management failures; Delhi's radar had no altitude readout.
probable_cause: The Kazakh Il-76 crew's failure to maintain its cleared altitude, worsened by poor English comprehension of ATC instructions and crew resource management failures, caused the collision with the climbing Saudia 747.

title: United Express 5925
summary: United Express Flight 5925 descended for landing at Quincy, a non-towered airport, on runway 13. A Beechcraft King Air began takeoff on intersecting runway 4 without proper monitoring of radio traffic. A GPWS sound in the United Express cockpit prevented the crew from receiving a complete transmission about aircraft holding positions. Both aircraft collided at the runway intersection and caught fire. All 14 occupants died from smoke inhalation.
probable_cause: King Air pilots' failure to effectively monitor the common traffic advisory frequency and scan for traffic. Contributing factor: simultaneous transmission by Cherokee aircraft that blocked the United Express crew's awareness.
